incidents.name: Wormhole
incidents.note: Signature verification bypass on cross-chain VAA messages

steps.description: Attacker initiates a legitimate withdrawal of 100 ETH on Chain A's bridge contract. The validators sign this withdrawal message using EIP-712 structured data. However, the bridge's domain separator omits the chainId field, making the signature valid on any chain with the same contract address.

The validator set signs the withdrawal message hash. The signed message contains the recipient, amount, and nonce — but because chainId is missing from the domain separator, this signature is equally valid on Chain A and Chain B. The validators unknowingly create a replayable authorization.

state_changes.signature_chain_binding: ⚠️ NONE — valid on any chain with same contract

steps.description: Attacker executes the legitimate withdrawal on Chain A, receiving 100 ETH. This is a normal, valid transaction. The attacker carefully records the complete signed message and all validator signatures from the transaction calldata.

Attacker replays the exact same transaction on Chain B (Arbitrum). Because the domain separator is identical (no chainId), the signatures are valid. The nonce 42 hasn't been used on Chain B yet. The bridge contract on Chain B verifies the signatures and releases another 100 ETH — a double spend.

state_changes.double_spend: ⚠️ 200 ETH total withdrawn from 100 ETH deposit

steps.description: The attacker can repeat this on every chain where the bridge is deployed with the same contract address and domain separator. Each chain is a fresh target. The total theft is multiplied by the number of chains, potentially draining the bridge's liquidity across all deployments.

state_changes.total_stolen: 💰 100 ETH × N chains (e.g., 500 ETH across 5 chains)
state_changes.root_cause: ⚠️ Missing chainId in EIP-712 domain separator
